The letter to the town hall

Thursday, 4 September 2036, evening, in Yves Le Goff’s little house in the small Breton harbour. Yves died at dawn. Nathalie has to write to the town hall to ask permission to scatter his ashes at sea, as he wished. Julien and Isabelle have come to help her.
He wanted his ashes scattered at sea, in front of the harbour. But we have to write to the town hall, and I don’t know how to write that kind of letter.
We’ll write it together. First the subject line: “Request for authorisation to scatter ashes at sea”.
And how do I start? “Hi, it’s Nathalie”? (she smiles sadly)
Not quite. “Madam Mayor,” then: “I take the liberty of approaching you in order to obtain…”
He’d have hated that style. He used to say: “Stop that thing of yours.”
Exactly. Unlike him, the town hall loves formulas. It’s the last favour you’re doing him.
Then you explain: “In accordance with the last wishes of the deceased, Mr Yves Le Goff…”
And what if she refuses? Supposing we have to wait for weeks?
She won’t refuse. As long as the request is complete, it’s a simple declaration. But we’ll state the date, just in case.
Saturday the 13th, at high tide. If the sea is calm. Otherwise, the Sunday.
And to finish: “I would be grateful if you would kindly examine my request. Yours faithfully, Madam Mayor.”
Even if it were the most beautiful letter in the world, he’d laugh at me.
Then add a handwritten postscript. In his own language. Nobody at the town hall will hold it against you.

Memory trick: “cas” and “hypothèse” take the conditional; “supposer”, “admettre”, “peu que” take the subjunctive.
2. Review: contrast
He wanted to go to sea, whereas everyone thought he was too weak. (alors que + indicative)
Unlike him, the town hall loves formulas.
Instead of crying, they sang. (au lieu de + infinitive)
The letter is very formal. On the other hand, the postscript is informal.
Don’t forget: “bien que” + subjunctive (concession), but “alors que” + indicative (contrast).

Le dernier quart

The phone call came on a Wednesday evening at the end of August 2036, while Julien was sorting the orchestra’s scores for the new season. It was Nathalie. Her voice was calm, too calm, the voice of someone who has already cried a great deal and has no tears left. She said Yves was unwell. That he refused to go to hospital. And that he wanted to see everyone one last time before he left.

Yves Le Goff was ninety-two. For three years he had lived in a small stone house on the quay at Le Croisic, with blue shutters and a view over the whole harbour. Nathalie, who lived twenty minutes away, had moved in with him at the beginning of the summer, when he could no longer manage the stairs. She slept in the little ground-floor room and made him galettes every Sunday, as he had taught her.

The two of them had become inseparable, so much so that the whole harbour thought they were married. They weren’t. Nathalie had been Ioana’s boss for fifteen years in Lyon before retiring to Brittany, and she had met Yves by chance, because of the waltz. He had taught her to sail. She had taught him to use a phone. Neither knew which had learnt more from the other.

Julien hung up and sat in the kitchen for a long time. He thought of the day he had first met Yves, in Nantes, five years earlier. The old sailor had handed him a cassette, saying simply: “It’s Henri. Dakar, 1978.” Without that cassette, nobody would ever have known where the waltz came from. Without Yves there would have been no Mariama, no Ibrahima, no little girl with the mess tin. Julien realised he owed him almost everything.

Julien, Ioana and the children set off on Saturday morning, with Isabelle. Six hours on the road. Henri-Ion asked forty times whether they were nearly there. Rose-Hélène asked nothing. She was eight and a half now, and she understood what people didn’t tell her. On her knees she held a cardboard box she had prepared for Yves. She hadn’t wanted to tell anyone what was inside.

On the way they stopped in Nantes, at the old shipyard on the banks of the Loire, where the network had planted a lime tree five years earlier. The tree had grown well. It shaded a bench where students were eating sandwiches. Rose-Hélène took out a bottle of water from the La Duchère fountain and poured it at the foot of the tree, as she did everywhere. Then she filled another bottle at the shipyard tap. She said it was for Yves. Water from Nantes, his city.

They reached Le Croisic in the late afternoon. The harbour was full of pleasure boats, tourists in shorts and screaming gulls. Nathalie was waiting for them outside the house with the blue shutters. She had grown thin. She hugged them one after another without a word. Then she said Yves was asleep, but had asked to be woken as soon as they arrived. He had said: “In case I don’t wake up on my own.”

Yves was lying in a bed that had been set up in the living room, in front of the big window overlooking the harbour. He had become very thin, very small, as if the sea had slowly worn him down over ninety-two years. But his eyes were the same: blue, mocking, lively. When he saw Rose-Hélène he smiled. He said: “Here’s the only person in the family who plays in tune.” Rose-Hélène replied that she didn’t play in tune at all. Yves said: “Exactly.”

Henri-Ion stayed in the living-room doorway, shy. Then he went up to the bed and asked the question the adults didn’t dare ask. He asked Yves whether he was going to die. Ioana tried to stop him. Yves raised his hand. He said yes, probably soon. Henri-Ion asked whether he was afraid. Yves thought about it. He said he had crossed the Atlantic forty-three times, and had been afraid every time at the start, never at the end. Henri-Ion nodded, reassured.

Rose-Hélène went up to the bed with her cardboard box. She put it on the blankets. Yves opened it with trembling hands. Inside there was a drawing, a dried lime twig and a small bottle of water. The drawing showed a boat on a blue sea, with an old sailor at the helm and a little girl in the bow. The twig came from the La Duchère lime tree. The water from the fountain. Rose-Hélène said it was so he could take a bit of Lyon with him.

Yves didn’t ask where he was supposed to take it. He knew. So did Rose-Hélène. He just laid his hand on the little girl’s head, very gently, the way you lay your hand on the helm of a boat you know well. Then he asked for the drawing to be put on the wall opposite the bed, where he could see it. Julien pinned it up next to an old chart of the Atlantic covered in pencil lines.

In the evening Nathalie made galettes, as on every Saturday. She served them with salted butter and cider on the living-room table, next to the bed, so that Yves could be with them. He ate only one mouthful. But he inspected every galette with a professional eye, and told Nathalie the third one was overcooked. Nathalie said that was a good sign: as long as he criticised her galettes, he was still here. Everyone laughed. So did Yves.

Each line on the chart was a voyage. Yves knew them all by heart. In the evenings, when the children were asleep, he told them to Julien and Isabelle, in a voice that grew weaker and weaker but with his memory intact. The first boat, in 1958, when he was fourteen and a ship’s boy on a trawler from Douarnenez. The storms of the winter of 1962. And Marseille, in 1971, the day he met a young sailor with a harmonica and two missing fingers.

Henri. Isabelle listened to these stories about her father the way you listen to music. She had hardly known Henri, who was always at sea when she was little. Yves had known him better than she had. He told her things she didn’t know: that Henri sang out of tune, like Odile; that he talked about his daughter to the whole crew; that he kept her photo in his shirt pocket, next to his heart, even during storms. Isabelle cried silently. Yves pretended not to see.

On Sunday morning Yves taught Henri-Ion to tie a bowline, the most important knot for a sailor. He could no longer move his arms, so he explained in words, and Henri-Ion tried with a piece of rope, sitting at the foot of the bed. “The rabbit comes out of the hole, goes round the tree and back down the hole.” It took forty minutes. On the thirty-seventh try, the knot held. Yves said Henri-Ion could now sign on to any ship in the world.

On Sunday, Amina and Bertrand arrived from Lyon with Awa, who was three and a half months old. Yves had asked to see her. He had said he wanted to meet the youngest member of the crew before leaving the ship. Amina laid the baby in his arms with care. Yves looked at her for a long time. Awa opened her big serious eyes. Then she grabbed the old sailor’s finger in her little hand and wouldn’t let go.

There were ninety-two years between them. The oldest and the youngest. Nobody in the room dared speak. Yves said in a low voice: “Welcome aboard, cabin girl.” Then he turned to Amina. He said he had something to ask her. A debt to settle. A promise he hadn’t kept. He asked Nathalie to open the chest-of-drawers drawer. She took out a packet of cigarettes, new, still in its cellophane.

Amina understood at once. Two years earlier, during the honeymoon in Dakar, she had put Yves in touch by phone with Ibrahima, the old docker of quay number four. Yves had promised to bring him a cigarette himself, to replace the one he had thrown him from the deck in 1978. He had never been able to make the trip. He had bought the packet the day after the call and kept it in that drawer for two years, waiting to get better.

He asked Amina whether her mother, Mariama, could take it to Dakar in his place. Amina said her mother was arriving on Wednesday, as it happened, to see him. Yves smiled. He said a sailor must never die with a debt, especially a cigarette debt, because in ports those are the most sacred. Then he added that Ibrahima didn’t smoke, he knew that. But that wasn’t the point. A promise was a promise.

In the afternoon, Bertrand stayed alone with Yves for a long time. He told him the story of his violin, hidden in the attic by his father in 1996 and returned by his mother when Awa was born. Yves listened without interrupting. Then he said Henri too had hidden something from his daughter all his life: a lock of hair, in a logbook. He said fathers often hid what they loved most, because they didn’t know how to say it. Bertrand said he would try to do better. Yves said: “You’re already doing better. You’re here.”

On Monday Yves asked for one last thing. He wanted to go out to sea. An hour, no more. The doctor, a serious young man who came by every morning, said it was impossible, he was far too weak, he might not come back. Yves replied that that was precisely the idea, but he would rather come back all the same, so as not to upset Nathalie. The doctor couldn’t tell whether he was joking. Nathalie could.

Although everyone thought he was too weak, Yves insisted. Nathalie finally called Loïc, a fisherman from the harbour who had sailed with Yves in the eighties and had kept an old wooden boat, the Marie-Jeanne. Loïc said yes without hesitating. He said he had been waiting for that call for months. If the sea was calm, they would go out on Tuesday morning at high tide. Otherwise they would wait. Yves said he didn’t have much time left for waiting.

The night before the trip, late, Yves asked Nathalie to promise him something. He wanted her to keep the house with the blue shutters. Not to sell it. To keep making galettes on Sundays, watching the harbour from the window, and answering when someone whistled on the quay. Nathalie promised. Then she asked what she would get in return. Yves said: “My woolly hat. And my place at the window.” Nathalie said it was a very good deal.

On Tuesday 2 September the sea was calm. Flat as a mirror, Loïc said, as if it had been warned. They carried Yves to the boat on a chair, four of them: Julien, Bertrand, Loïc and another fisherman. The whole harbour had stopped to watch. The tourists didn’t understand why the fishermen were taking off their caps. Yves was settled in the stern, wrapped in a blanket, his old woollen hat on his head. Nathalie and Rose-Hélène went aboard with him.

The Marie-Jeanne left the harbour slowly, her old engine coughing like a smoker. At the end of the jetty, Loïc cut the engine and raised the sail. The wind was light. The boat glided over the water without a sound. Yves asked to take the helm. Loïc hesitated, then handed it to him. For one minute, just one, Yves held the helm in his trembling hands. The boat stayed perfectly straight. Loïc said later he had never seen anyone steer so well.

Out at sea, Yves asked Rose-Hélène to play the waltz. She took out Henri’s harmonica, the one that had travelled with him for six years on the same ships. She played the first verse, then the second, facing the sea, standing in the bow, as in her drawing. Yves had his eyes closed. Nathalie held his hand. Loïc had taken off his cap. At the third verse, Rose-Hélène stopped. Eight bars. There was only the wind, the water against the hull, and gulls in the distance.

On the fifth bar, Yves whistled. Faintly, almost without breath, but in tune. For the first time in his life, according to Nathalie, he whistled in tune. Three notes. Then he opened his eyes and looked at the sea, the sky, the coast in the distance, Rose-Hélène in the bow. He said: “There. That’s good. We can go back.” Loïc started the engine again. They went back into harbour under a soft September sun, without a word. On the quay, people were waiting. They applauded.

After the trip, Yves slept for fourteen hours straight, a calm, deep sleep, without moving. The doctor, who had come in the morning fearing the worst, found him more rested than he had been for weeks. He said he couldn’t understand it. Nathalie explained that for a sailor, the sea was the best medicine. The doctor said that wasn’t in any textbook. Nathalie said that was a shame for the textbooks.

Mariama arrived from Dakar on Wednesday afternoon, straight from Nantes airport by taxi. She was sixty-eight; she had seen Yves only once, at the opening of the exhibition, and had spoken to him several times on the phone. But she had wanted to come. She said she owed it to the sailor who had thrown a cigarette to her uncle Ibrahima in 1978, while she listened to the harmonica with her mess tin. Ibrahima wasn’t really her uncle. But in Dakar, all the old dockers were uncles.

Yves recognised Mariama at once. He said: “The little girl with the mess tin.” Mariama sat on the edge of the bed and took his hand. They talked for a long time in low voices, about Dakar, the quay, that evening in 1978 they had both lived through without seeing each other, he on the deck, she on the quay. Yves gave her the packet of cigarettes. He asked her to tell Ibrahima he was sorry for the delay. Fifty-eight years’ delay. Mariama promised.

On Wednesday evening Isabelle took out her cello, which she had brought from Lyon without knowing whether she would play it. She sat at the foot of the bed. She asked Yves what he wanted to hear. He said: “Not the waltz. I know it by heart. Something Henri didn’t know.” Isabelle played a Bach sarabande, slowly, in the shadowy living room, with the window open onto the harbour. Outside on the quay, people stopped to listen. Yves fell asleep before the end.

That night, the night of 3 to 4 September, Yves didn’t sleep. Nor did Nathalie. She sat beside him in the dark, with the window open onto the harbour. You could hear the halyards of the boats clinking against the masts, the lapping of the water, a gull now and then. The others were asleep upstairs, or pretending to be. Around four, Yves asked the time. Nathalie told him. He asked whether the tide was coming in. She said it was.

Around six, when the sky began to pale above the sea, Yves opened his eyes one last time. He looked at Rose-Hélène’s drawing on the wall: the boat, the old sailor, the little girl in the bow. He said, very softly, to Nathalie: “It’s time for my watch.” Nathalie replied: “Go on. I’ll take over.” He smiled. He closed his eyes. He died at twelve minutes past six, at the exact moment the tide turned.

Nathalie stayed sitting beside him until sunrise. Then she went upstairs to wake the others, one by one, without a sound. Rose-Hélène woke first. She didn’t need anyone to explain. She came down in her pyjamas, went up to the bed and looked at Yves for a long time. Then she took out the harmonica and played the three notes very softly. Nobody answered. She said it didn’t matter. He had already answered, on the boat.

During the morning the news went round the harbour. Loïc came by, cap in hand. Then other fishermen, one after another, without coming in, just to touch the door with the blue shutters. Around noon, all the boats in the harbour lowered their flags to half-mast. Tourists asked what was going on. An old fisherman told them a sailor had gone. Not died, he said. Gone. Among sailors you never say one of your own has died. You say he has gone.

That same evening the paperwork had to be dealt with. Yves had planned everything, the way a sailor prepares his boat before a storm. In the chest of drawers, next to where the packet of cigarettes had lain, there was an envelope with his last wishes, handwritten in his old sailor’s slanting hand. He wanted to be cremated. He wanted his ashes scattered out at sea in front of the harbour. And he wanted the waltz to be played. “Badly, preferably,” he had added.

To scatter the ashes at sea, they had to write to the town hall. Nathalie, who had run an architecture firm for thirty-five years and drafted hundreds of official letters, suddenly no longer knew how to begin. She said she felt as if she were writing to the town hall to ask permission to say goodbye. Julien and Isabelle sat down with her at the kitchen table. They wrote the letter together, sentence by sentence, until midnight.

It was a perfect letter. A subject line, a salutation, three paragraphs, a closing formula. “I take the liberty of requesting.” “In accordance with the last wishes.” “I would be grateful.” “Yours faithfully.” Nathalie reread it three times. Then she said Yves would have hated every word. So she took a pen and added, by hand, at the bottom of the page, a postscript in Yves’s own language. She wouldn’t show it to anyone before sending it.

The mayor of Le Croisic replied two days later. An official letter, with the town hall’s stamp, authorising the scattering of the ashes on Saturday 13 September at high tide, and stating that no further declaration was needed for the boats. And at the bottom of the letter she too had added something by hand. A single line, in round handwriting: “I read your postscript. On Saturday, I’ll whistle too.”

Rose-Hélène spent the afternoon writing a letter to Yves. She wrote it on a sheet of exercise paper, taking great care, without a single mistake. She wouldn’t show it to anyone. Then she folded it into a little boat, as Yves had taught her the summer before. She said she wouldn’t put it in the sea, because paper caused pollution. She would keep it in the harmonica box. That way the letter would travel with the music.

The news of Yves’s death went round the network in one evening. It reached Brest, where the musicians of La Criée played the waltz that same night in the great hall whose ribbon he had cut. It reached Corsica, Bucharest, Dakar, Mirecourt. Gérard Thiébaut announced he would come, despite his eighty-three years and six hours on the train. The Brest bagad asked whether they could play on the quay. Nathalie said yes to everyone.

But it was the harbour of Le Croisic itself that surprised everyone. On Monday, Loïc came and knocked on the door with the blue shutters. He said the harbour’s fishermen had talked it over. They wanted to accompany Yves. All of them. With their boats. Nathalie asked how many there were. Loïc said there would be about forty, maybe more if the yachtsmen joined in too. He added that the last time the harbour had done that was in 1974, for a shipwreck.

Léonie Garnier called to ask whether she could film the ceremony. Nathalie hesitated for a long time. Then she said no. Kindly but firmly. She said Yves had spent his whole life seeing things nobody filmed: dawns over the Atlantic, whales off Iceland, storms in the middle of the night. He would have wanted his departure to be the same. Léonie said she understood. She came anyway, without a camera, with her triangle.

On the eve of the ceremony the messages kept arriving. Viorica, from Bucharest, writing in violet ink that sailors and pianos had in common that they sounded better with age. Paul Delmas, who had met Yves at the film premiere and sent three drawn notes. Hortense Valmont, from the Académie, quoting a line of Baudelaire about free men and the sea. And Sami, who had written a short text for Yves and read it over the phone, in verlan, in French and in harbour slang, all at once.

On Saturday 13 September, at daybreak, there was fog over the whole harbour. A thick white fog that hid the boats ten metres away. Rose-Hélène woke at six and ran to the window. She was afraid the ceremony would be postponed. Nathalie reassured her. She said September fog always lifted with the tide. As long as the wind turned, it would disappear within an hour. Rose-Hélène asked how she knew. Nathalie said: “He taught me.”

At ten o’clock the fog lifted all at once, like a curtain. The sun appeared over the sea. And the whole harbour appeared with it: forty-three fishing boats and yachts, decked with flags, lined up along the quays, their crews standing on deck. On the jetty there were hundreds of people. Harbour folk, musicians from the network, families, strangers from all over Brittany. And in front of them, the Brest bagad in traditional dress.

Nathalie went aboard the Marie-Jeanne with the urn, a simple urn of pale wood that Gérard Thiébaut had made himself in his Mirecourt workshop, from the wood of an old broken violin. With her were Loïc at the helm, Rose-Hélène, Isabelle, Julien and Mariama. The others boarded the fishermen’s boats. Bertrand, Amina and Awa on a blue trawler. Ioana and Henri-Ion on a sailing boat. Gérard Thiébaut, too tired to embark, stayed on the jetty with the mayor.

When the Marie-Jeanne left the quay, the bagad began to play. It was the waltz. But not as anyone had ever heard it: played on Breton bagpipes and bombardes, with drums, slow, solemn, almost like a march. The forty-three boats followed the Marie-Jeanne, one behind the other, in a long line leaving the harbour. On the jetty, people fell silent. All you could hear was the bagad and the engines.

Out at sea, at the exact spot where Yves had held the helm eleven days earlier, Loïc cut the engine. The other boats arranged themselves in a circle around the Marie-Jeanne, slowly, without a word, as they had agreed among themselves. Forty-three boats in a circle on a calm, shining sea. On the jetty in the distance, the bagad was still playing. Rose-Hélène stood up in the bow, as in her drawing. She took out the harmonica. She waited for the bagad to reach the end of the second verse.

Then everything stopped. The bagad on the jetty. The engines of the forty-three boats, cut at the same moment. The conversations. Even the gulls, Loïc said later, but nobody believed him. Eight bars. Out at sea, in the middle of the circle, Nathalie opened the urn. She poured the ashes into the water, slowly. The wind carried them out to sea, westwards, towards the Atlantic Yves had crossed so many times. Rose-Hélène poured the little bottle of La Duchère water over them.

On the fifth bar, a foghorn sounded. Then another. Then all the others. Forty-three foghorns together in the middle of the sea, a huge deep sound that rolled all the way to the coast. On the jetty, people jumped. Some cried. It was the only note the boats knew how to play. They played it all together, for an old sailor, in the middle of the silence. Then the horns fell silent, and only the sea remained.

At the end of the eight bars, Rose-Hélène played the three notes on the harmonica, facing the open sea. And from the jetty in the distance, someone answered by whistling. Then hundreds of people. Then the bagad, which took up the waltz where it had left off. On the jetty, the mayor of Le Croisic was whistling, as she had promised. Beside her, Gérard Thiébaut was whistling too, leaning on his cane. And on the blue trawler, in her mother’s arms, Awa woke up and smiled.

On the way back, Loïc beckoned Rose-Hélène to the stern. He put the helm in her hands. She was frightened. He laid his big hand over hers, and they steered together, slowly, to the harbour entrance. Rose-Hélène looked straight ahead, very serious, her tongue between her teeth. Loïc told Nathalie the girl had the knack. Nathalie smiled for the first time in ten days. She said it ran in the family.

The Marie-Jeanne came back into harbour last, after all the others. On the quay, people stepped aside to let it through. When Nathalie set foot on land, the mayor came towards her. She was a woman of about sixty, in a yellow oilskin, who had been a fisherwoman before being elected. She shook Nathalie’s hand. She said she had been moved by the letter, but above all by the postscript. She said she would keep it in the town hall register. As an official document.

In the evening there was a big party in the harbour bistro, as Yves had asked in his last wishes: “No speeches, songs.” The fishermen sang sea shanties in Breton and French, banging on the tables. Bertrand played the violin. The bagad played outside on the quay. Nathalie had made three hundred galettes that afternoon, with the help of half the women in the harbour. Nobody said the third one was overcooked. Everyone thought it.

The next day Mariama flew back to Dakar, with the packet of cigarettes in her handbag, wrapped in a scarf. She took the plane from Nantes, then from Paris. Throughout the flight she kept the bag on her knees, the way Mrs Lacroix had once kept the 1950 letter. In Dakar, Moussa was waiting at the airport. She asked him to drive her straight to the harbour. Not home. To the harbour. To quay number four.

Ibrahima was there. He was eighty-four now. He came to the quay every day, leaning on his cane, to watch the ships. The guards had long since let him in. When he saw Mariama coming, he understood at once. He knew Yves had died; Lamine had told him. But he didn’t know about the packet. Mariama handed it to him. She repeated Yves’s words: “Sorry for the delay.” Ibrahima looked at the packet for a long time without a word.

Then he removed the cellophane slowly, with his old docker’s fingers. He took out a cigarette. He had never smoked in his life. He asked a passing young docker for a light, who gave it to him with wide eyes. Ibrahima went up to the old rusty bollard, the one Henri’s ship had been moored to in 1978. He lit the cigarette. He took a puff. And he coughed and coughed, doubled over, for a good minute.

When he had finished coughing, he was laughing. He laughed so loudly that the dockers on the quay stopped to look at him. He told Mariama it was the most disgusting thing he had ever tasted, and that he finally understood why he had kept the other one for fifty years without smoking it. Then he laid the lit cigarette on the bollard, facing the sea. The smoke rose gently towards the sky, then the wind carried it out to sea, northwards, towards Brittany.

Ibrahima watched the smoke until the cigarette had burnt down completely. Then he said something in Wolof that Mariama later translated for Nathalie over the phone: “He kept his word. Late, but he kept his word. Among sailors, that’s all that counts.” He put the packet back in his pocket, with the nineteen remaining cigarettes. He said he would smoke one every year, on 4 September, on this quay. And that he would cough every time. For Yves.

In Lyon, the following Thursday, Bernard Delorme arrived at rehearsal with an enormous parcel. He opened it in front of the whole orchestra. It was a real ship’s foghorn, red, bought online. He announced that from now on, on the fifth bar of the silence, alongside Amina’s triangle, there would be the foghorn, for Yves. Théo said it was impossible, it was far too loud. Bernard tried it. Every alarm in the neighbourhood went off. Théo said yes anyway.

At Le Croisic, Nathalie stayed in the house with the blue shutters. She didn’t want to go home. She said she had taken over the watch, and you didn’t leave your post in the middle of a watch. One evening, sorting Yves’s things, she found his last logbook, the one he still kept, even ashore, like Henri. The last page was dated 2 September, the day of the trip out to sea. There were only a few words, in a very shaky hand.

“2 September. Calm sea. Light westerly wind. Helm held one minute. The little one played the waltz in the bow. Silence observed. End of my watch. Relief assured.” Underneath he had drawn three musical notes. Nathalie closed the logbook. She put it on the windowsill, facing the harbour, next to the old woolly hat. Then she opened the window. Outside, someone on a boat was whistling three notes while stowing their nets. Nathalie answered.

Objet : demande d’autorisation de dispersion de cendres en mer

Madam Mayor, I take the liberty of addressing this letter to you in order to request authorisation to scatter at sea the ashes of Mr Yves Le Goff, who died on 4 September 2036 at his home, aged ninety-two.

In accordance with his last wishes, expressed in writing, a copy of which you will find enclosed, Mr Le Goff wished his ashes to be scattered out at sea off the harbour, where he had begun sailing in 1958.
The ceremony would take place on Saturday 13 September, at high tide, should weather conditions permit. Otherwise it would be postponed to the following day.
Several boats from the harbour have offered to accompany the deceased. I would be grateful if you would kindly let me know whether a further declaration is required for them to go out.
I remain at your disposal for any further information. Looking forward to your reply, I remain, Madam Mayor, yours faithfully. — Nathalie Fabre
P.S. (handwritten): He always said the sea asked nobody’s permission. But he was polite. So I’m asking it for him. And if you hear whistling on Saturday, don’t worry: it’ll be us.
